items.title: ARIFICIAL INTELLEGENCE AND ENGLISH READING MOTIVATION INFLUENCING COMMUNICATION SKILLS AMONG PAKISTANI UNDERGRADUATE COLLEGE STUDENTS
items.abstract: The fast incorporation of artificial intelligence (AI) into higher education has changed how university students’ access, evaluate, produce, and communicate scientific information. At the same time, English reading motivation remains significant for Pakistani college undergraduate students because English is extensively used in academic, educational, lingua franca and scientific contexts. English language is also enjoying prestigious status in Pakistan. This study examines AI literacy and English reading motivation as predictors of science communication skills among Pakistani students. AI literacy is theorized as students’ ability to understand, use, evaluate, and ethically engage with AI technologies, while English reading motivation refers to students’ interest in reading for educational, academic and other purposes. Science communication skills include the skill to explain scientific concepts accurately, clearly, ethically, and appropriately to in this context with multi socio-economic and culture backgrounds of Pakistan. Existing literature suggests that AI literacy involves more than technological usage and includes critical evaluation and ethical awareness. Likewise, research on English-medium instruction indicates that language competence can influence students’ participation and learning experiences. This study has used a quantitative, correlational-predictive design involving collegiate students from Pakistani higher education institutions. Data have been collected from N=250 college students through standardized questionnaires and a science communication performance task. Descriptive statistics, Pearson correlations, and multiple regression analysis have been completed. The study shows that there are evidences for assimilating AI literacy, English proficiency, and science communication into college programs.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence (AI) and the 2027 Elections: Comparing Urban and Rural Voters' Responses to AI-Generated Campaign Messages in Abia State, Nigeria
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is entering Nigerian electoral communication ahead of the 2027 general elections, raising concerns about authenticity, trust and misinformation. This exploratory study examined how voters aged 18–40 in Abia State, Nigeria, understand, feel about and respond to AI-generated and AI-assisted campaign messages, and how urban/semi-urban and rural voters compare. Method: A qualitative exploratory design was adopted. Twenty voters (ten urban/semi-urban and ten rural) were purposively selected from communities across Abia State and interviewed individually using six AI-generated or AI-assisted campaign materials (CM1–CM6), supplemented by observation notes. Data were analysed through reflexive thematic analysis and interpreted with the Elaboration Likelihood Model. Findings: AI familiarity varied within both groups rather than simply between them. Participants separated emotional appeal from credibility, and realistic fabrication caused more concern than obvious satire. The messages stimulated attention, discussion and verification more readily than candidate support, and rural participants relied more on interpersonal and community verification networks. Conclusion: Within this sample, AI-generated campaign messages shaped electoral judgement through credibility, emotional appeal, realism and verification conditions rather than automatic vote conversion. As exploratory findings, these are not statistically generalisable but offer propositions for larger studies.

items.title: Artificial intelligence (AI) anxiety and nurses’ turnover intention during healthcare digital transformation: the mediating role of occupational fatigue
items.abstract: Background The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into healthcare is associated with new psychological challenges. However, the extent of its impact on nursing workforce stability is unclear. Aim To explore the relationship between AI anxiety and turnover intention of clinical nurses, and the mediating effect of occupational fatigue and the moderating effect of emotional intelligence (EI). Methods A cross-sectional survey was conducted from March to June 2026 among 404 clinical nurses from four hospitals in Jiangsu Province, China. Data were collected using the AI Anxiety Scale (AIAS), Health Workers’ Occupational Fatigue Scale (HWOFS), Turnover Intention Scale (TIS) and Wong and Law Emotional Intelligence Scale (WLEIS). Mediation was tested using structural equation modelling with bootstrap resampling, while moderation was tested using moderated regression analysis. Results Differences in baseline turnover intentions across age, department, and professional title level were statistically significant (all p < 0.001). Path analysis showed that AI anxiety was positively associated with occupational fatigue (β = 0.611, p < 0.001) and turnover intention (β = 0.530, p < 0.001). Occupational fatigue partially mediated the association between AI anxiety and turnover intention (indirect effect = 0.299, 95% CI: 0.129, 0.379). EI had a significant negative main effect on occupational fatigue (b = −0.257, p < 0.001), but it did not significantly moderate the association between AI anxiety and occupational fatigue. Conclusion AI anxiety is significantly correlated with the turnover intention of clinical nurses, and occupational fatigue may represent a potential pathway linking AI anxiety and turnover intention. Although EI is associated with lower levels of occupational fatigue, it fails to cushion the impact of AI anxiety, a specific stressor. Hospital administrators should focus on targeted AI literacy improvement plans and specific fatigue relief strategies to retain clinical nursing staff.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Digital Health in the Diagnosis of Leprosy: Current Advances and Future Perspectives
items.abstract: Leprosy remains a significant public health challenge in endemic regions, where delayed diagnosis leads to irreversible nerve damage, disability, and ongoing transmission. To address the need for innovative diagnostic strategies, artificial intelligence (AI) and digital health technologies have emerged as promising tools. This review explores the current applications of machine learning, deep learning, computer vision, and mobile health platforms in leprosy diagnosis and management. AI-based image analysis demonstrates strong potential for identifying characteristic skin lesions and differentiating leprosy from other dermatological conditions. Additionally, predictive algorithms and smartphone-based telemedicine expand access to specialized care in underserved settings while facilitating contact tracing, surveillance, and treatment monitoring. Despite these encouraging advances, significant challenges remain, including limited high-quality annotated datasets, algorithmic bias, a lack of external validation, and data privacy concerns. Ultimately, AI-driven digital health solutions should complement rather than replace clinical expertise. Prioritizing multicenter collaborations, explainable AI models, and secure data integration will be essential to strengthen global leprosy control programs, improve patient outcomes, and reduce the burden of this neglected tropical disease.

items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly recognized as a general-purpose technology with significant implications for economic growth, employment, financial stability, and national security. This article examines how AI reshapes economic security, understood as the capacity of households, firms, and states to withstand shocks to income, markets, and critical infrastructure. Using a structured narrative review of academic research, international policy reports, regulatory frameworks, and technical safety studies, the article identifies four principal risk domains: labor-market disruption, market concentration and infrastructure dependence, financial instability, and malicious or geopolitical misuse. The review also examines governance challenges arising from fragmented regulatory approaches, limited institutional capacity, incomplete evidence, and the rapid pace of technological deployment. The findings indicate that AI-related risks are interconnected and that vulnerabilities can spread through shared models, concentrated computing infrastructure, and correlated institutional decisions. In response, the article proposes a layered resilience framework combining adaptive regulation, competition policy, financial supervision, workforce investment, and international coordination. It concludes that economic security depends not only on preventing harmful applications of AI but also on strengthening institutions’ ability to anticipate, absorb, and recover from technological shocks.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Hybrid Optimization Techniques for Non-Traditional Machining: A Comparative Review of Recent Advances and Applications
items.abstract: Non-traditional machining (NTM) processes—electrical discharge machining (EDM), electrochemical machining (ECM), laser beam machining (LBM), abrasive water jet machining (AWJM), and ultrasonic machining (USM)—are indispensable for producing geometrically intricate features in hard-to-cut super alloys, ceramics, and composites. Their governing physics are stiff, coupled, and non-stationary, making first-principles real-time control prohibitively expensive. This review surveys how machine learning surrogates—multilayer perceptron’s (MLPs), Gaussian process regression (GPR), adaptive neuro-fuzzy inference systems (ANFIS), and physics-informed neural networks (PINNs)—and hybrid meta-heuristic optimizers—particle swarm optimization fused with gravitational search (PSO-GSA), and NSGA-III with reference-point decomposition—are being deployed to bridge the gap between laboratory models and shop-floor control. We present the formal governing equations for each process, compare surrogate architectures on five engineering-relevant axes, and synthesize published performance improvements across six NTM modalities in a standardized table. Critical attention is given to small-data generalization failure, the inadequacy of Ra as a surface-integrity proxy, and the architectural requirements for deploying inference on embedded FPGA/PLC controllers.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and IoT-Enabled Chemical Pollution Monitoring and Remediation of Rivers: A Comprehensive Review of Sensing Technologies, Machine Learning Methods, and IoT Integration
items.abstract: Rivers receive chemical contamination from industrial effluent, domestic sewage and agricultural runoff, including nutrients such as phosphorus, organic load, and other pollutants. Conventional assessment relies on periodic sampling and laboratory analysis, which needs specialised staff, chemicals and expertise, and therefore cannot give continuous, early warning of pollution events. Artificial intelligence (AI), combined with low-cost sensing and the Internet of Things (IoT), is increasingly proposed for continuous river monitoring and for the data-driven control of chemical treatment such as coagulant dosing. This paper presents a focused narrative review of studies that use machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) with IoT sensing for river water quality monitoring and chemical-treatment control. It examines three connected themes: sensing technologies, learning methods, and IoT architectures. The reviewed literature reports water-quality classification accuracy of up to 98 % with an Arduino-based IoT device, XGBoost-based prediction in an industrially affected river basin, ML-assisted phosphorus sensing in river samples, and a deep-learning coagulant-dosing model that reduced dosage by about 22 % in a plant study. However, most studies are small, single-site, short-term and laboratory-oriented, and few report field validation, sensor fouling and drift, or closed-loop treatment control in rivers. The paper contributes a comparative table of representative studies, a conceptual river-to-decision architecture (not experimentally validated), and a prioritised list of research gaps.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Robotics: The Future of Humanity, Mass Unemployment, Hunger, and the Global Economic Crisis
items.abstract: Abstract This working paper examines the potential economic and social consequences of accelerating artificial intelligence, robotics, and large-scale automation, with particular attention to technological unemployment, income insecurity, wealth concentration, declining purchasing power, food insecurity, and social instability. It addresses a fundamental question: What happens when machines can produce an increasing share of the goods and services humanity needs, while large numbers of people lose the employment income required to purchase those goods and services? The paper explores how automation may transform employment across agriculture, manufacturing, construction, transportation, commerce, professional services, and knowledge-based occupations. It considers the possibility that productivity gains may become increasingly concentrated among the owners of advanced technologies, while affected workers and households experience economic insecurity. Particular attention is given to developing and low-income countries, where limited household savings, informal employment, weak social protection systems, and restricted public resources may amplify the consequences of rapid technological displacement. Rather than assuming that mass unemployment, hunger, or social unrest are inevitable, the paper presents alternative future scenarios for 2036–2045 and identifies economic, institutional, and social conditions that could increase or reduce these risks. It proposes a preventive policy framework incorporating international open vocational transition institutes, proactive workforce reskilling, social funds supported by productivity and capital returns, income protection mechanisms, food security safeguards, economic early-warning indicators, and contingency plans for large-scale employment disruption. The paper calls upon researchers, governments, universities, international organizations, labor institutions, and technology companies to investigate these risks before technological displacement exceeds the capacity of societies to adapt. The central concern is not whether machines will become more productive than human beings, but whether humanity can develop economic and social institutions that ensure the benefits of technological progress remain accessible to all. This publication is an exploratory working paper and public policy proposal. It does not claim to establish a new technological discovery, present a validated economic model, or demonstrate that widespread unemployment or social crises are inevitable. items.title: Artificial Intelligence and the Smart Mobility Nexus: A Systematic Evidence Review
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly reshaping transportation through predictive analytics, intelligent infrastructure, connected mobility, autonomous systems and energy-responsive transport management. This systematic evidence review examines the AI-smart mobility nexus with an emphasis on intelligent transportation infrastructure and operational sustainability. Following PRISMA 2020, 30 eligible sources published between 2015 and 2026 were synthesised from Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, ScienceDirect and Google Scholar. The corpus comprised 29 review, survey, meta-review, bibliometric or conceptual syntheses and one case study; accordingly, evidence was interpreted qualitatively and no pooled effect estimates were calculated. Five dominant domains emerged: AI-enabled traffic management, connected transportation infrastructure, safety and risk reduction, electric and renewable-energy-integrated mobility, and operational sustainability. Across the included literature, AI was generally associated with improved prediction, routing, incident recognition, system coordination, infrastructure monitoring and energy-management capability, although transferability depended on data quality, connectivity, infrastructure readiness, grid capacity and institutional capability. Operational efficiency did not consistently imply broader environmental or social sustainability. Interpreted through Technological Innovation Systems and Sustainability Transition perspectives, the evidence suggests that sustainable smart mobility depends on coordinated technological, infrastructural, institutional and energy-system development. The review therefore supports a qualified conclusion: AI can contribute to safer and more efficient mobility, but stronger primary, longitudinal and geographically diverse evidence is needed to establish durable environmental and social outcomes.

items.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AND VOCAL BIOMARKERS IN ASTHMA DIAGNOSIS AND MONITORING: A NARRATIVE REVIEW
items.abstract: Considering that chronic respiratory diseases, such as asthma, represent a global challenge, their continuous monitoring is often limited by the need for specialized equipment. Artificial Intelligence (AI) applied to the acoustic analysis of cough and voice emerges as a non-invasive alternative. It aims to investigate how vocal biomarkers can be isolated for the specific detection and monitoring of asthma. To this end, we proceed to a narrative review that synthesizes recent literature on the application of machine learning algorithms. In this way, it is observed that changes in respiratory mechanics modify extractable acoustic parameters, such as MFCCs. Several architectures demonstrate high accuracy, frequently exceeding 85% to 90% by fusing spectral and temporal features. Data augmentation tools overcome sample scarcity, and advanced filters mitigate ambient noise on smartphones. This allows us to conclude that AI-processed vocal biomarkers hold significant clinical potential for outpatient screening. The standardization of recording protocols and validation in multicenter cohorts are essential for the safe integration of this technology into telemedicine.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Approaches for Gastrointestinal Bleeding Detection in Capsule Endoscopy: A Systematic Review and Critical Analysis
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: Gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding is a common, potentially life-threatening condition, and capsule endoscopy (CE) is the principal investigation for suspected small-bowel bleeding after non-diagnostic upper endoscopy and colonoscopy. Because manual review of thousands of CE frames is labor-intensive, artificial intelligence (AI) has been proposed to automate bleeding detection. Methods: Following PRISMA 2020, this systematic review synthesizes 15 peer-reviewed journal studies (2020–2025) applying traditional machine learning, convolutional neural networks, transfer learning, attention-based or hybrid architectures, segmentation, or object detection to GI bleeding detection in CE. Methodological quality was appraised with an AI-adapted risk-of-bias framework informed by QUADAS-2 and PROBAST. Results: Frame-level classification accuracy ranged from 90.6% to 99.9% (median 98.5%; 13 studies), with the lowest values from evaluations closest to clinical practice; the segmentation and detection studies reported a mean intersection-over-union of 86.9% and an mAP@0.5 of 79.0%. Only two studies (13%) were at low risk of bias for validation strategy, none reported patient-level separation of training and test data, only four (27%) used clinical patient data, and none compared AI with conventional endoscopy or clinical outcomes. Conclusions: Current evidence demonstrates high performance on curated datasets but not yet generalizability or clinical readiness; patient-level, external, and prospective multicentre validation is required.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence for Crop Pest Detection: A Review of Deep Learning Techniques, Challenges, and Future Directions
items.abstract: Pests reduce both the yield and the quality of crops, and checking fields by hand is slow, tiring, and dependent on trained experts. Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly computer vision and deep learning, makes it possible to recognize pests from photographs and to respond to infestations earlier and with better precision. This review looks at AI-driven pest detection in terms of image classification, object detection, public benchmark datasets, model efficiency, and practical deployment. A focused narrative search of scholarly sources and publisher pages was carried out, covering work on the IP102 benchmark, the Pest24 dataset, machine-learning and deep-learning surveys, YOLObased pest detectors, and rice-pest detection. The literature shows that convolutional neural networks can learn the visual cues needed for pest classification, while object detectors from the YOLO family can find and label several pests within one image. The choice of dataset strongly shapes how trustworthy an evaluation is: IP102 holds more than 75,000 images in 102 categories, with bounding boxes for roughly 19,000 of them, whereas Pest24 consists of field images in which pests are small and often packed closely together. Newer model-specific studies report gains on the test sets they selected, but figures drawn from different datasets and evaluation protocols cannot be compared head to head. Challenges that keep recurring include tiny pests, look-alike species, imbalanced classes, cluttered field backgrounds, changing light, a shortage of labelled field data, and the limited computing power available on devices. The review points to the need for more representative field testing, open evaluation practices, efficient models, reporting of uncertainty, and stronger links between detection output and integrated pest management. AI-based detection is promising, yet a high benchmark score alone does not prove dependable performance on real farms. Future work should focus on external validation, ease of use for farmers, and responsible use of model predictions.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence for Emergency Department Triage and Risk Stratification: A Review
items.abstract: Researchers increasingly investigate artificial intelligence (AI) as a tool to support triage and early risk stratification in emergency departments. However, improved predictive performance does not necessarily translate into safer decisions or better patient outcomes. This critical narrative review examines the evidence for AI in adult ED care, with particular emphasis on prospective evaluation, patient safety, and clinical implementation. The review compares conventional triage systems, early warning scores, and clinician assessment with machine learning, natural language processing, and large language models. It examines commonly used data inputs, prediction timing, model discrimination, calibration, external validation, and the limitations of outcome definitions. Attention is given to the distinction between predicting clinical deterioration, critical care need, short-term mortality, and hospital admission. Evidence is considered across retrospective development, external validation, silent prospective evaluation, clinician-visible implementation, and randomized trials. AI may help identify patients requiring closer assessment by integrating information from multiple sources. Nevertheless, its clinical value depends on data quality, timely predictions, generalizability, and healthcare professionals' ability to interpret outputs appropriately. Important risks include under-triage, automation bias, unequal performance across patient groups, and increased clinical workload. Prospective studies and randomized trials are therefore essential to establish whether AI-supported decisions improve patient outcomes compared with usual care. Future research should prioritize multicenter clinical evaluations, consistent outcome reporting, subgroup assessment, and continuous monitoring after deployment. AI implementation should also include clear accountability, human oversight, and procedures for reviewing adverse events. Evidence of predictive accuracy alone is insufficient to justify routine adoption. Clinical integration should depend on demonstrated safety and meaningful benefit for patients.

items.title: Artificial intelligence for facial soft‐tissue landmark localization, measurement, and classification in orthodontics: A systematic review
items.abstract: Abstract This systematic review provides a broad overview of three distinct applications of artificial intelligence (AI) in facial soft‐tissue assessment: landmark localization, automated facial measurement, and classification of soft‐tissue conditions in orthodontic and dentofacial evaluation. PubMed, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, ClinicalTrials.gov, Google Scholar, and Open Science Framework were searched. Studies using 2D facial photographs, 3D facial scans, or AI‐generated facial models were included. Risk of bias was assessed with an adapted QUADAS‐2 tool and certainty of evidence with GRADE. The protocol was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261452521). Fifteen studies were included. Landmark‐localization performance varied substantially by imaging modality, landmark definition, data set, reference standard, and error metric; central and anatomically well‐defined landmarks were generally more accurate than peripheral or subjective points. Agreement for AI‐derived measurements ranged from poor to excellent, with ICCs of approximately 0.01–0.984. Classification accuracy ranged from approximately 0.83 to 0.98, with AUCs up to 0.98. Given only two narrowly scoped classification studies, these findings should be considered exploratory and hypothesis‐generating rather than broadly generalizable. Because of substantial methodological heterogeneity, findings were synthesized qualitatively. items.title: Artificial Intelligence for Scientific Discovery: A Focused Review of Large Language Models for Scientific Literature, Table Understanding, and Numerical Reasoning
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to accelerate scientific discovery, from predicting protein structures and molecular properties to extracting knowledge from the scientific literature. A large share of experimental evidence in papers is reported in numerical tables, yet automated analysis of such tables remains difficult. This paper presents a focused narrative review of verified sources on AI for scientific discovery, concentrating on large language model (LLM) based understanding of scientific text, scientific tables and numerical reasoning. It examines three connected themes: knowledge extraction and question answering over scientific text, table question answering benchmarks, and reasoning methods (direct prompting, chain-of-thought, program-of-thought, self-consistency and graph-based reasoning). The literature shows that scientific table benchmarks have moved from mostly lookup tasks towards a 1,607-question benchmark that requires multi-step numerical reasoning; on it, GPT-4.1 mini reached only 27.0 exact match under direct prompting on the computation-and-language subset, chain-of-thought prompting raised this to 71.5, and accuracy still fell from 74.6% on small tables to 59.2% on large ones. However, the evidence is concentrated in computer science tables, depends on LLM-generated and LLM-filtered questions, and agreement among human verifiers was only moderate (Fleiss' kappa 0.55). The review contributes a comparative analysis of benchmarks and methods, a proposed conceptual architecture linking extraction, cell selection, stepwise reasoning, verification and expert review, and a prioritised list of research gaps.

items.title: Artificial intelligence for vascular minimally invasive surgery: techniques, clinical integration, and challenges
items.abstract: Introduction Minimally invasive surgery (MIS), including endovascular and robot-assisted procedures, is widely used for vascular pathologies but remains limited by technical complexity, cognitive workload, and postoperative complications. Artificial Intelligence (AI) may help address these challenges through predictive analysis, decision support, image analysis, and automation. Methods A structured Google Scholar search was conducted from February 21, 2025, to January 1, 2026, and updated through September 2026. Peer-reviewed studies applying AI to vascular MIS were included, with additional targeted searches addressing clinical translation, deployment, regulation, and ethical considerations. Results Thirty primary studies were analyzed, including eight on machine learning, nine on deep learning, four on natural language processing, and nine on robotics or reinforcement learning. Machine learning supported risk stratification and outcome prediction, deep learning enabled imaging and segmentation applications, natural language processing facilitated clinical information extraction, and robotic systems supported navigation and procedural assistance. Discussion AI demonstrates substantial potential across the vascular MIS pathway, but broader clinical adoption requires stronger validation, prospective multicenter studies, standardized reporting, health-economic evaluation, and careful consideration of regulatory, liability, and accessibility challenges.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Agricultural Teaching, Research, and Skill Development for Sustainable Development in Nigeria
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is reshaping agricultural education globally, but its integration in Nigeria remains in its early stages. This chapter focuses on systematically embedding AI into Nigeria’s agricultural education through pedagogical innovation, institutional readiness, and skills development. Instead of broadly surveying AI’s role, it critically analyzes the necessary frameworks, practices, and policies for its operational inclusion in agricultural training and research. Drawing from empirical evidence and global models (India, Kenya, Brazil, and China), the chapter explores AI-enhanced pedagogies, such as smart learning environments and digital simulations, to bolster competencies in precision agriculture, climate-smart farming, and agribusiness management. The analysis identifies four key dimensions for AI integration: curriculum redesign for competency-based learning; institutional capacity and infrastructure; ethical governance of digital systems; and alignment with Nigeria’s Digital Economy and AI Strategies. While awareness and pilot initiatives are on the rise, challenges like weak infrastructure, limited staff training, and fragmented policy implementation restrict large-scale adoption. The chapter proposes a phased integration model—encompassing awareness, capacity building, curriculum reform, and adaptive feedback—to facilitate sustainable transformation. Ultimately, it argues that AI should be regarded not just as a technological innovation but as a pedagogical framework vital for transforming Nigeria’s agricultural education ecosystem. By aligning AI with national sustainability goals, Nigeria can develop a new generation of digitally skilled, sustainability-focused agricultural professionals prepared for the challenges of the twenty-first-century food system.

items.title: Artificial intelligence in construction management: a systematic review of techniques, applications and data practices
items.abstract: Purpose This study presents an integrated systematic mapping of artificial intelligence (AI) applications in construction management, clarifying technique-domain pairings, data and validation practices, and deployment readiness across the construction lifecycle, addressing fragmentation in prior reviews. Design/methodology/approach Following the preferred reporting items for systematic reviews and meta-analyses (PRISMA) guidance for study identification and screening and the structured literature review approach, 148 peer-reviewed articles published between 2007 and 2025 across 14 journals were analyzed through bibliometric and thematic synthesis. An open companion web application (https://cm.electriai.com/) was developed, providing bibliometric visualizations, a searchable paper database, and a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) AI assistant. Findings The review shows that AI research in construction management accelerated after 2022 but remains uneven in its technical and methodological development. Technique-domain mapping revealed lock-in patterns: vision-based deep learning (DL) was concentrated in safety, and traditional machine learning (ML) in cost estimation, while optimization, graph neural networks (GNNs), and generative AI remained underexplored. Data constraints persist: 40.5% of studies used datasets below 500 samples, 65.5% relied on private or unreported data, cross-project validation appeared in 1.4% of papers, and explainable AI (XAI) appeared in 3.4%. Practical implications Construction stakeholders require coordinated investment in open benchmark datasets, cross-project validation protocols, XAI integration and interoperable standards for building information modeling and Internet of Things systems. Originality/value This review integrates AI techniques, construction domains, data and validation practices, supported by an open companion web application for verifying, filtering, and querying the evidence base.

items.title: Artificial intelligence in healthcare and human resource management: a review of the global divide, Pakistan's landscape and institutional innovations
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping healthcare and organizational management worldwide, yet its benefits remain unevenly distributed between high-income and low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). This review examines the structural drivers of this global AI divide, situates Pakistan's healthcare and digital infrastructure challenges within this context, and presents an institutional case study of four AI-enabled interventions implemented at the Sindh Integrated Emergency and Health Services (SIEHS), an emergency and health services organization under the Health Department, Government of Sindh, Pakistan: an AI-driven recruitment and candidate-job matching system (Talent Match Live), a facial-recognition and geolocation-based field monitoring application, an AI-assisted CCTV training-monitoring system, and an AI-augmented telemedicine triage service embedded within SIEHS's Teletabeeb telehealth department. Each intervention is evaluated against comparable systems documented in the international literature to assess feasibility, evidence of effectiveness, and associated ethical risks. A responsible-adoption framework is proposed to guide organizations in resource-constrained settings toward AI integration that is effective, equitable, and ethically governed. The review concludes that while AI offers meaningful efficiency and access gains for LMIC public-sector organizations such as SIEHS, sustainable adoption requires deliberate attention to data protection, algorithmic bias, workforce consent, and alignment with international ethical guidance.

This study has proved that the adoption of AI technology in post-primary educational sectors can be an effective strategic mechanism towards the goal of SDG 4. items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Middle and Secondary Education: Instructional Opportunities, Limitations and Ethical Considerations
items.abstract: Middle and secondary school educators should utilize and implement Artificial Intelligence (AI) as a support tool for instruction, not a replacement for their pedagogy and lesson planning. Utilizing and implementing AI can assist with lesson planning, differentiation, feedback, and generating learning materials; and its uses should be guided by clear expectations, professional judgment, and school policy. Educators should also teach their students how to use AI ethically, verify outputs for accuracy and bias, and protect student privacy by avoiding sensitive data. Most importantly, assessments should be designed to show genuine student understanding, with AI used transparently and appropriately. The best available published advice concurs that the usage of AI within an educator’s pedagogy significantly enhances middle and secondary school students’ learning. This article offers practical guidance for educators who use or plan to use AI in the classroom, while also highlighting policy recommendations to support effective educational practices.

items.title: Artificial intelligence in pharmaceutical drug product quality control and assurance
items.abstract: Abstract Machine learning has moved from proof of concept to routine operation in pharmaceutical quality control, yet the autonomy it is granted narrows sharply as products approach release. In this narrative review, we propose that this unevenness reflects not model capability but the regulatory burden an output must clear before it can be acted on, a pattern we term the validation‐barrier gradient. We score this barrier across four stages on criteria covering decision criticality under good manufacturing practice, validation and data‐integrity load, locus of legal liability, and patient‐safety consequence. The composite barrier rises as observed autonomy falls. At final product inspection, deep vision systems already detect defects at line speed, often on small single‐site datasets, but the authority to release a batch still rests with a qualified person. This gap between what a model can do and what it is allowed to decide cannot be explained by task difficulty alone. Closing it requires not further accuracy gains but shared benchmarks, routine robustness reporting, and change‐control pathways allowing validated models to be updated rather than frozen.

items.title: Artificial intelligence in religious education: teacher perspectives from a national professional development context
items.abstract: Abstract This study examines teachers’ perceptions of and orientations to Artificial Intelligence (AI) in the context of Religious Education (RE), drawing on survey data collected from 54 in-service RE teachers participating in the SUB8 professional development programme in Greece. Using a descriptive survey design grounded in the frameworks of Pedagogical Content Knowledge (PCK), Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK), AI literacy, and digital self-efficacy, the study maps teachers’ reported practices, competencies, and concerns across seven thematic dimensions. Findings indicate generally positive orientations towards AI-assisted instructional design within this cohort, alongside significant theological and pedagogical concerns regarding its use in spiritually sensitive contexts. Qualitative responses point to three recurring themes: the productive utility of AI for lesson preparation and differentiation; persistent concerns about accuracy, depth, and the reliability of AI-generated content; and a strong consensus that AI must function as a supplementary pedagogical tool, subordinate to the relational and experiential dimensions of RE. Because participants were self-selected members of an AI-focused training programme and were surveyed immediately upon its completion, these findings are interpreted as descriptive of this specific professional development context rather than of Greek RE teachers in general. The study complements recent comparative evidence from Germany and Poland by providing, to the author’s knowledge, the first empirical account of AI perceptions among RE teachers within an Orthodox national professional development context, and it foregrounds a theological and epistemological dimension still largely absent from AI-in-education research.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Talent Acquisition: An Empirical Assessment of Recruitment Outcomes and Responsible Use
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to source applicants, display screening packages, match candidates, communicate with applicants, and analyse workforce data. Processing speed alone does not indicate whether it is AI-powered. Recruitment outcomes also include shortlist relevance, applicant delight, recruiter productivity, and high-quality decisions. This study examines the relationship between AI adoption and five perceived skill-acquisition outcomes, drawing on questionnaire responses from 70 individuals. The analysis uses descriptive statistics, Cronbach's alpha, Pearson correlation, and separate simple linear regression. AI adoption undoubtedly improves recruitment performance (β = 0.546, R2 = 0.282), recruitment effectiveness (β = 0.514, R2 = 0.295), perceived candidate experience (β = 0.569, R2 = 0.363), recruiter productivity (β = 0.498, R2 = 0.329) and overall performance of talent acquisition (β = 0.341, R2 = 0.120). All five regression relationships are statistically significant at the 5% level. Candidate experience has the highest R2 among the five factors, while specific skill acquisition performance has the lowest. Additionally, respondents who report greater AI adoption tend to report more favourable recruiting outcomes, but the study does not establish causality or confirm changes in overall objective hiring performance. The article discusses these findings in relation to fairness, transparency, confidentiality, and human oversight. It recommends that firms assess the use of multiple end-result markers in AI-enabled hiring and conduct meaningful human assessment of the resulting options.

items.abstract: This study examined artificial intelligence (AI) integration, management effectiveness, and school–enterprise collaborative talent training at Guangzhou Huali Vocational College of Science and Technology, China. A descriptive-correlational quantitative design involved 159 students and 101 teachers during the second semester of academic year 2025–2026. Students were included through total enumeration and teachers through purposive sampling. A researcher-developed questionnaire was validated by five experts and pilot-tested with 30 individuals; Cronbach’s alpha was 0.96. Analysis used frequencies, percentages, weighted means, t tests, one-way analysis of variance, and Pearson correlations. Both groups rated AI integration as high, management effectiveness to a high extent, and training success to a high degree. Students’ assessments differed significantly by enterprise exposure across all three constructs; teachers’ AI integration assessments differed by position. AI integration correlated positively with management effectiveness for students (r = 0.8839) and teachers (r = 0.9225). Management effectiveness correlated positively with training success for students (r = 0.9399) and teachers (r = 0.9586). The findings support coordinated curriculum, assessment, supervision, faculty development, and workplace learning. A Comprehensive AI Integration Framework was proposed to strengthen institutional practices and collaborative training. The relationships indicate association rather than causation.

items.title: Artificial intelligence literacy and innovative behavior among clinical nurses: the roles of AI self-efficacy and organizational innovation climate
items.abstract: Objective To investigate the current status and related factors of innovative behavior among clinical nurses in tertiary hospitals and explore the relationships and pathways among artificial intelligence literacy, AI self-efficacy, organizational innovation climate, and nurse innovative behavior, for providing a basis for targeted nursing management strategies. Methods This cross-sectional study was conducted on 850 nurses from six tertiary medical institutions using a stratified survey approach in Yueyang city, Hunan province, from June to July 2026, in the General Information Questionnaire, Artificial Intelligence Literacy Scale, Artificial Intelligence Self-Efficacy Scale, Organizational Innovation Climate Scale, and Nurse Innovative Behavior Scale were used. AMOS 24.0 was used to conduct confirmatory factor analysis to assess the model fit of the scales. SPSS 26.0 was used for descriptive statistics, univariate analysis, Pearson correlation analysis, and multiple linear regression. PROCESS macro version 4.2 Models 4 and 14 tested mediation and moderated mediation effects. Results A total of 850 valid questionnaires were obtained, with a valid questionnaire rate of 95.3%. The mean nurse innovative behavior score was 37.93±6.50. The measurement model for the four scales showed good fit, and the scales demonstrated good convergent validity and some evidence of discriminant validity. Artificial intelligence literacy, artificial intelligence self-efficacy, organizational innovation climate, and innovative behavior showed positive associations with one another (r = 0.609–0.797, P < 0.01). Educational level, professional title, participation in research or innovation activities, artificial intelligence literacy, artificial intelligence self-efficacy, and organizational innovation climate were factors associated with nurse innovative behavior and explained 60.9% of the total variance. Artificial intelligence self-efficacy partially mediated the relationship between artificial intelligence literacy and nurse innovative behavior. The indirect effect was 0.322, with a 95% CI of 0.243–0.403, accounting for 52.90% of the total effect. Organizational innovation climate moderated the relationship between artificial intelligence self-efficacy and nurse innovative behavior (b = 0.051, P < 0.01). The index of moderated mediation was 0.041, with a 95% CI of 0.009–0.078. Conclusion AI literacy was closely related to nurse innovative behavior, with AI self-efficacy as a partial mediator and organizational innovation climate as a moderator. Nursing management may focus on AI competencies, application confidence, and organizational support.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Readiness in Bangladesh’s Public Administration: Linking Digital Leadership, Employee AI Capability, and Service Innovation
items.abstract: AI will emerge as a significant force behind administrative change, although public organisations vary in their preparedness to do so. This paper investigates the impact of digital leadership and employee AI ability on artificial intelligence preparedness and innovation in services in the Bangladesh public administration. A four-reflective construct survey model was created, including digital leadership, employee AI capability, AI readiness, and service innovation. It was analysed with a synthetic dataset of 835 cases that are intended to test the methodology and prove PLS-SEM. The data were evaluated using descriptive statistics, common method bias tests, evaluation of the measurement model, structural model, mediation, and predictive assessment. The findings revealed that the positive impacts of digital leadership and employee AI capability on AI preparedness were significant. Service innovation was also positively impacted by AI readiness significantly. Digital leadership and employee AI capability had a direct impact on service innovation. Both relationships were partially mediated by AI readiness. The model explained 45.4% of the variance in AI readiness and 41.0% of the variance in service innovation. All the predictive relevance values were positive and the PLS model yielded lower prediction errors than linear benchmark. The results reveal a readiness pathway that is coherent where leadership, employee capability, and institutional preparedness contribute to innovation in the delivery of public services.

items.title: Artificial intelligence use patterns, attitudes, and psychological distress among medical students: a cross-sectional survey
items.abstract: Background Artificial intelligence (AI) tools are widely used by medical students, but associations of general use frequency and AI-related attitudes with psychological distress remain unclear. Methods All 1,275 active students at one Turkish medical faculty were invited to an anonymous online survey conducted from 1 April to 1 May 2026; 249 of 251 respondents consented. Measures included general AI use, an investigator-translated 13-item Artificial Intelligence Attitude Scale (ATAI), and the validated Turkish Depression Anxiety Stress Scales-21. A general-distress composite was the primary outcome, and hierarchical regression used HC3 robust standard errors. Results AI use was reported by 95.6% of participants, and 50.2% reported daily use. Mean doubled DASS-21 total was 56.97 (SD 31.55). The ATAI three-factor model showed mixed fit (CFI = .898, TLI = .872, RMSEA = .107, SRMR = .070). AI-frequency categories did not improve the adjusted model at the block level (change in R -squared = .016, p = .111; robust global p = .088). Adding exploratory ATAI factors increased R-squared by.052 ( p = .002; robust global p = .009); Benefit was inversely, and Risk and Use positively, associated with distress. Subscale sensitivity analyses preserved coefficient directions, but only the inverse Benefit-Anxiety association survived correction across 15 additional focal tests ( q = .032). Conclusion AI use was nearly universal and served both educational and personal/non-educational purposes, but this sample did not provide stable evidence of an overall association between general use frequency and distress. ATAI associations are exploratory and may reflect measurement or common-method processes. Longitudinal multicenter studies should use formally adapted measures and objective indicators of AI engagement.

items.abstract: Background: Cancer screening plays a crucial role in early diagnosis and improved survival, yet conventional screening methods are limited by false-positive findings, false-negative results, interobserver variability, delayed reporting, and unequal access to expert interpretation.Objective: To review recent advances in artificial intelligence-assisted cancer screening, focusing on applications in radiology, histopathology, and liquid biopsy.Methodology: This narrative review summarized published evidence on the role of artificial intelligence, machine learning, and deep learning in cancer screening.The review focused on three major domains: AI-assisted radiology, AI-assisted histopathology, and AI-assisted liquid biopsy.Results: AI-assisted radiology has shown value in lesion detection, image classification, risk stratification, and workflow prioritization, particularly in breast and lung cancer screening.In histopathology, AI supports tumor detection, grading, biomarker quantification, margin assessment, and reduction of interobserver variability.In liquid biopsy, AI improves interpretation of circulating tumor DNA, circulating tumor cells, methylation markers, microRNAs, and other molecular biomarkers for early cancer detection and tumor-origin prediction.Conclusion: Artificial intelligence has considerable potential to strengthen cancer screening by improving early detection, diagnostic accuracy, efficiency, and individualized risk assessment.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence-Based Human Behavior Analysis for Reducing Cybersecurity Risks and Human Errors
items.abstract: Human behavior remains one of the most persistent contributors to cybersecurity incidents, as unintentional errors, social-engineering susceptibility, and insider misuse continue to bypass purely technical safeguards. This conceptual, literature-based study examines how artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) techniques can be applied to analyze human behavioral patterns in order to reduce cybersecurity risk and human error within organizational information systems. Drawing on a structured review of insider-threat detection, phishing and social-engineering research, security-awareness training studies, and explainable-AI literature, the study synthesizes recurring behavioral indicators, modeling approaches, and evaluation practices reported across the field. A conceptual AI-based human-behavior-analysis framework is proposed, comprising data acquisition, behavioral feature engineering, AI/ML modeling, explainable risk scoring, and adaptive human-in-the-loop response. The review indicates that sequence-aware deep-learning models, such as long short-term memory networks and autoencoders, combined with explainable AI techniques, achieve strong reported detection performance while preserving analyst interpretability, and that adaptive, behavior-based training interventions are associated with measurably greater reductions in human-related risk than static, one-time awareness programs. The study concludes that integrating continuous behavioral analytics with human-centered training and feedback mechanisms offers a more resilient approach to cybersecurity risk management than technology-only or training-only strategies. Implications for organizational security governance, model interpretability, and future empirical validation are discussed.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence-Based Study Notes Generation Using Generative AI and Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Comprehensive Review of Retrieval Methods, Prompting, Educational Evidence, and System Architecture
items.abstract: Learners often spend a great deal of time condensing lecture slides, textbook chapters and research papers into brief revision notes. Large language models (LLMs) from the generative AI family can draft such notes within seconds, but a model that is not grounded in a source may write confident text that the material never states. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) lowers this risk by supplying the model with passages fetched from the learner’s own documents. This paper offers a focused narrative review of verified literature on AI-driven study notes generation with generative AI and RAG. Three linked areas are covered: retrieval and RAG techniques (chunking, dense embeddings, retrievers and advanced pipelines); generative models and prompting (LLMs, structured prompt frameworks and hallucination); and empirical evidence on generative AI in engineering and computing courses. The reviewed work indicates that RAG was proposed to anchor generation in retrieved text, that dense retrieval outperformed a strong sparse baseline in open-domain question answering, and that in a quasi-experiment with 26 students, structured prompts produced fuller answers than free-style prompts. Even so, most educational studies capture student perceptions instead of learning outcomes, rely on small samples, and none of the reviewed studies directly measures note quality, faithfulness or retention. The paper contributes a comparison of representative studies, a conceptual seven-layer architecture that links ingestion, retrieval, grounded generation, verification and learner feedback, and a ranked list of research gaps.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Bone Fracture Assessment: A Comprehensive Review of Imaging and Sensing Technologies, Machine Learning Methods, and Clinical Integration
items.abstract: Bone fractures are among the most common musculoskeletal injuries, and their outcome depends on accurate classification, timely localisation and early recognition of failed healing. Manual radiograph interpretation is subjective and time-consuming, and plain X-ray is slow to reveal healing failure (nonunion), which affects up to 12 % of tibial fractures and can take more than six months to diagnose [1]. Artificial intelligence (AI), combined with medical imaging and novel sensing, is increasingly proposed as a route to fast, consistent and early fracture assessment. This paper presents a focused narrative review of four verified peer-reviewed IEEE Access studies (2022–2025) covering contactless antenna-based sensing of implant deflection and fracture stiffness, X-ray fracture-type classification with transfer learning and ensemble classifiers, two-stage CT-based cervical spine fracture classification and vertebra detection, and attention-enhanced YOLOv8 detection of paediatric wrist fractures. The review examines three connected themes: imaging and sensing technologies (X-ray, computed tomography and near-field electromagnetic sensing), learning methods (CNN transfer learning, hybrid CNN–classical ensembles and object detectors), and clinical integration with explainability. The literature shows that deep models can classify fracture types with about 95–98 % accuracy, that YOLOv8 variants reach about 93.5 % mAP50 for vertebra detection and 65.8 % mAP50 over all wrist-trauma categories, and that a miniaturised Vivaldi antenna (36 × 30 mm) can track sub-millimetre implant displacement. However, most studies use single-source datasets, small test sets, random data splits and offline evaluation, and few report clinical validation. The review contributes a comparative analysis of representative studies, a proposed conceptual architecture linking acquisition, AI inference, decision support and clinical reference validation, and a prioritised agenda of research gaps and future directions.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Smart Milk Quality Assessment: A Comprehensive Review of Sensing Technologies, Machine Learning Methods, and IoT Integration
items.abstract: Milk is a highly perishable, high-value food whose quality is affected by natural compositional variation, economically motivated adulteration with water, sugars, starch, urea or melamine, microbial spoilage during storage and transport, and udder diseases such as mastitis. Reference methods, including laboratory Fourier-transform infrared (FTIR) analysis, microbiological culture and chromatography, are accurate but centralised, slow and costly, which restricts routine testing at farm and collection-centre level. Artificial intelligence (AI), combined with rapid sensing and the Internet of Things (IoT), is increasingly proposed as a route to fast, on-site and continuous milk quality assessment. This paper presents a focused narrative review of verified peer-reviewed studies, prioritising 2022–2026 publications, that use AI for milk composition prediction, adulteration detection, spoilage assessment and udder-health prediction. The review examines three connected themes: sensing technologies (mid-infrared, near-infrared and fluorescence spectroscopy, low-cost multispectral chips, electronic noses and smartphone-based vibration sensing), learning methods (partial least squares chemometrics, classical machine learning such as support vector machines, random forests and gradient boosting, and deep learning such as convolutional neural networks), and IoT architectures with edge and cloud inference. The literature shows that spectroscopic data with machine learning or deep learning can detect single adulterants with reported accuracies of about 95–100 %, and that inexpensive 18channel spectral sensors calibrated against laboratory FTIR can estimate fat and protein with mean errors of about 0.07–0.14 %. Simple, interpretable models often perform as well as complex ones. However, most studies use small, single-region datasets, laboratory conditions, single adulterants and random data splits, and few report field validation, sensor drift, uncertainty or long-term IoT operation. The review contributes a comparative analysis of representative studies, a proposed conceptual farmto-plant architecture that links multi-sensor acquisition, edge AI, IoT decision support and laboratory reference validation, and a prioritised agenda of research gaps and future directions.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence: Learning Flow in 30 Years
items.abstract: The rapid ubiquity of generative artificial intelligence (AI) has fundamentally disrupted traditional pedagogical frameworks in engineering education, necessitating a critical examination of its impact on cognitive development and knowledge retention. This longitudinal study spans 30 years (1996–2025) to analyse shifts in student learning curves within an AI curriculum, testing the hypothesis that reliance on automated tools exacerbates a ‘J-curve’ learning style, characterised by delayed engagement and terminal production spikes, at the expense of fundamental understanding. By comparing weekly topic acquisition and final assessment data across cohorts, the research reveals a distinct morphological transformation from the classic sigmoidal progression (‘S-curve’) of the baseline 1996 class to an exponential ‘J-curve’ in the 2025 cohort. While modern students demonstrate high procedural efficiency in project delivery, this shift correlates strongly with a significant decline in independent examination performance, where mean scores fell from 9.50 to 7.75. Although a gradual decline in performance was observed prior to 2020, the disruption caused by the COVID-19 pandemic and the subsequent ubiquity of generative AI tools may have intensified this trend (main finding). The data indicate that students utilise AI to bypass the cognitive friction necessary for deep learning, resulting in a failure to exit the assisted phase of skill acquisition. These findings suggest that current AI integration acts as a mechanism for cognitive offloading rather than scaffolding, creating a trade-off between immediate output and long-term declarative competence. The study concludes that engineering curricula must rigorously re-evaluate assessment strategies to ensure that the efficiency of automated generation does not erode the foundational logic required for sustainable innovation.

items.title: Assessing the Usability of Existing ITS Data for Autonomous-Driving AI: A Task-Specific Framework for Sustainable Data Reuse
items.abstract: This study assesses whether existing intelligent transportation system (ITS) data can be reused for autonomous-driving artificial intelligence (AI) based on task-specific information requirements and the recoverability of missing information. A task-specific framework was applied to five heterogeneous ITS data assets—roadside closed-circuit television (CCTV), camera-based and radar-based automatic incident detection system (AIDS) data, radar-based smart intersection system (SIS) data, and vehicle detection system (VDS) performance-evaluation data—across four data-use tasks: 2D road-user detection training, detection/measurement output validation, event/structured traffic-state retrieval, and road-referenced trajectory reconstruction. For each asset–task pair, mandatory information requirements were identified and classified as explicitly available, directly derivable or linkable, recoverable through feasible transformation, not reliably recoverable, or unconfirmed; these information-level states were then translated into task-specific usability. The results showed that usability varied substantially by task. Camera-based AIDS provided the broadest direct usability, whereas roadside CCTV showed greater reuse potential through transformation. Radar-based AIDS, radar-based SIS, and VDS performance-evaluation data were directly usable for validation and structured traffic-state retrieval, while visual-training and trajectory-reconstruction usability was more limited. Performance-evaluation records showed particular value for validation because they preserved target outputs, validated reference information, and their correspondence. These findings demonstrate that the reuse value of existing ITS data depends on the information actually retained and its recoverability rather than on sensing modality alone. By identifying reusable data and selective future-retention needs, the framework supports more resource-efficient management of digital ITS assets and links task-specific data reuse to sustainable transportation.

items.title: Assessing the Use, Impact, and Perspectives of Generative Artificial Intelligence Among Health Consumers: A Cross-Sectional Survey in Saudi Arabia
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: Saudi Health consumers increasingly rely on generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) to access health information from a growing number of health-related resources. Little is known about the frequency and patterns of generative AI tool use for seeking health information among consumers, its reported impact, and health consumers’ perceptions of these tools. This study aims to investigate the use of and perspectives on generative AI tools among health consumers in Saudi Arabia (SA). It also aims to assess the impact of their use on health-seeking behaviours. Methods: An exploratory, cross-sectional, self-administered online survey was distributed to adults (≥18 years) residing in SA during two data collection rounds in 2026 (March–April and July–August). All adults who used generative AI tools to seek online health information in the past year were included. Bivariate and multivariate analyses were conducted to examine relationships among variables. Results: A total of 403 eligible health consumers (58% male) participated. Among respondents who had used generative AI for health purposes, approximately 49% reported using it more than five times per month. Younger age, higher income, and more frequent pre-use were associated with higher odds of frequent seeking health information behaviour. Headache, abdominal pain, and musculoskeletal pain were the most common claims. ChatGPT was the main platform (84%) used for seeking information. Age was significantly negatively associated with frequency, whereas income and pre-visit use were positively associated. The primary reasons for seeking health information via generative AI were quick information retrieval (71%), time saving (34%), and curiosity (30.5%). Conclusions: The high frequency of use suggests that generative AI can serve as a source of health information and may lead users to withhold health information from healthcare providers. It may influence subsequent health-seeking behaviours, such as requesting urgent care or postponing physician visits. These self-reported findings do not establish diagnostic accuracy, clinical effectiveness, or patient safety, and the clinical risk and appropriateness of self-management actions were not assessed. Many respondents reported concerns about inaccurate information, missed serious illness, and increased health anxiety.

items.title: Association of ambient artificial intelligence scribe availability with patient instruction documentation and readability in ambulatory care
items.abstract: Abstract Objective This retrospective cohort study evaluated the effect of an artificial intelligence (AI) scribe on patient instructions documentation in ambulatory internal medicine settings. Materials and Methods We analyzed 391 061 adult encounters at a single medical center from December 2023 to July 2025. A difference-in-differences analysis estimated the relationship of AI scribe availability with patient instructions documentation frequency. Mixed-effects logistic regression estimated the association between encounter-level AI scribe utilization and documentation, adjusted for patient, clinician, and encounter characteristics. Length and readability were compared across instructions created by AI alone, clinicians assisted by AI, and clinicians alone. Character-level edit distances between AI drafts and final documentation were calculated. Results AI scribe availability was associated with a 10.5 percentage-point increase in patient instructions documentation frequency (P = .018), and encounter-level AI use was associated with higher odds of documentation (aOR 4.32; 95% CI, 4.14-4.50). AI instructions were longer than clinician-authored content (median 1994 vs 482 characters) and scored higher on 3 text-complexity indices (all P < .001). Clinician editing of AI content increased length without meaningfully reducing complexity. AI drafts and final documentation differed substantially, with a median character-level edit distance of 39.7%. Discussion AI scribe availability was associated with increased patient instructions documentation. However, AI-generated instructions were longer and scored as more linguistically complex than clinician-authored instructions, and clinician editing did not close this gap. Conclusion Ambient AI scribes can improve availability but may increase complexity of patient instructions. Research into downstream effects including patient comprehension and satisfaction is warranted.

items.title: Athlete-AI: a multi-modal artificial intelligence framework for personalized athlete monitoring and injury risk forecasting
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) provides opportunities for computational athlete monitoring, adaptive training analysis, and injury-risk modelling. This study presents Athlete-AI, a multimodal AI framework that integrates wearable sensor data, human motion information, pose features, and literature-derived athlete variables into a unified computational architecture. The framework combines multimodal feature fusion, reinforcement learning for adaptive training simulation, and machine-learning-based injury-risk modelling. The evaluation was conducted using publicly available benchmark datasets, including PAMAP2, Human3.6 M, and Microsoft COCO, together with literature-derived parameters used to construct simulated athlete profiles, workload, fatigue, recovery, and injury-risk scenarios. The framework was evaluated through computational experiments and simulation-based athlete-monitoring scenarios to examine multimodal integration, injury-risk classification, and adaptive training behaviour. Repeated-run evaluation across five random seeds, probability-calibration analysis, component ablation, comparison with multimodal fusion baselines, and a leakage-controlled analysis of the dependence on label-defining variables were also performed. When the workload, fatigue, recovery, and biomechanical-risk variables used to define the simulated labels were removed from the predictors, the F1-score decreased from 86.6 to 72.8%. Negative-control analyses showed that the benchmark-derived features-only model produced performance comparable to the shuffled-label control. The results demonstrate the computational feasibility of integrating heterogeneous athlete data and evaluating adaptive training and injury-risk modelling within a unified simulation environment. The reported performance values represent preliminary computational results and do not constitute real-world, clinical, or prospective athlete validation. Therefore, the proposed framework should be regarded as a computational research framework that requires validation with longitudinal data from real athletes before practical or clinical deployment.

items.title: Atlas: Making Sense of Long Horizon Agent Trajectories
items.abstract: AI agents can now search literature, generate hypotheses, analyze datasets, and run experiments at a scale difficult for researchers to match. Yet scaling scientific execution does not automatically scale researchers' ability to make sense of what agents produce. When researchers return to a long-horizon run, they must evaluate work they did not monitor: what the agent produced, which decisions shaped those outputs, and whether those decisions served the research goal. We frame this post-run sensemaking as a representation problem across three linked levels: goal, decision, and artifact. From this framework we developed Atlas, an agentic workspace with a trajectory tree, which renders the run as a branching structure showing what the agent chose and set aside, and artifact projections over six representations. In a within-subjects study (N=14), participants reported higher decision transparency, artifact sensemaking, and goal connection with Atlas than with a standard baseline, together with substantially lower subjective workload.

The review will use structured academic searches, predefined eligibility criteria, transparent study selection, quality appraisal and comparative narrative synthesis. Reporting will be guided by PRISMA 2020 and PRISMA-S, with methodological consideration of established software-engineering systematic review guidance. items.title: Automating quantum circuit optimization with AI agents
items.abstract: Compiling quantum algorithms for real devices involves hard optimization problems that can decide whether an algorithm runs at scale. We present a general method for solving such problems with AI agents, with every result certified. It builds on autoresearch loops, in which agents iteratively improve programs against a fixed evaluator and which have recently improved quantum cryptanalysis circuits, and adds two elements: a frozen, exact verifier certifies every result, and this verifier, together with the challenge around it, is built by an agent that formulates the problem with a researcher and validates the verifier against a solved case, deliberately broken solutions and published results before any solution exists. The method applies to any optimization problem whose solutions can be verified exactly and efficiently. We apply it to three compilation problems in quantum simulation, namely fermion-to-qubit encoding, Hamiltonian layout and unitary synthesis. In each, the agents improved substantially on published or standard constructions, reducing the cost being optimized by up to 73% at the largest sizes tested and outperforming a state-of-the-art optimizer for fermion-to-qubit encodings. Every submission is a program accompanied by its agent's notes, so the ideas behind each improvement are recorded in human-readable form; later agents built on them, and we describe them here. These results open the way to automated, certified discovery across quantum circuit design and beyond.

items.title: Automation of quality audits in healthcare services through information systems: a scoping review
items.abstract: This protocol describes a scoping review aimed at mapping the scientific literature on computerized systems, with or without artificial intelligence (AI), that automate quality auditing processes in healthcare services. Quality auditing supports patient safety and the identification of nonconformities; however, it is often a manual process based on data extraction from medical records and checklists organized in spreadsheets, placing a substantial workload on Quality Departments. Computerized systems, such as audit software, dashboards, rule-based systems, robotic process automation (RPA), machine learning, and natural language processing, have the potential to reduce this workload, improve information traceability and the resolution of nonconformities, and support evidence-based decision-making. However, the available evidence on this topic is scattered and heterogeneous, and no previous or ongoing reviews addressing this subject have been identified. The review will follow the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology and the PRISMA-ScR guidelines, with searches conducted in national and international databases and grey literature sources, without restrictions on language or publication year. Study selection and data extraction will be performed by two independent reviewers, and the results will be presented in tables, figures, and an evidence map, accompanied by a narrative synthesis. The analysis will seek to characterize the systems, the quality dimensions audited, the technologies employed, and the benefits, barriers, and limitations associated with their implementation. Thus, the review is expected to identify knowledge gaps and inform future research and technological development in this emerging field.

items.title: Autonomous AI-Driven Security Operations Centers (Autonomous SOC): Agentic Orchestration, Real-Time Incident Response, and Multi-Agent Defensive Playbooks
items.abstract: Abstract—Contemporary enterprise Security Operations Centers (SOCs) are on the brink of systemic collapse driven by three converging factors: exponential alert fatigue (>25,000 uninvestigated alerts daily per enterprise), acute global cybersecurity workforce shortages, and the emergence of automated, machine-speed cyber threats executing multi-stage Advanced Persistent Threats (APTs) in sub-minute time horizons. Traditional Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response (SOAR) platforms rely on brittle, rigid, hard-coded linear playbooks that fail when adversaries deviate slightly from known MITRE ATT&CK patterns. The paradigm of the Autonomous AI-Driven SOC (Autonomous SOC) establishes a transformative architecture that replaces rigid rule engines with specialized collaborative Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) powered by fine-tuned Large Language Models (LLMs) and Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). In an Autonomous SOC, decentralized cognitive agents autonomously triage alerts, execute deep forensic graph correlation, synthesize non-linear incident playbooks, isolate compromised endpoints via zero-trust API invocations, and conduct automated counter-adversarial negotiations. However, deploying autonomous agentic execution in mission-critical defensive infrastructure exposes severe risks: catastrophic hallucination loops during remediation, prompt injection propagation across defensive pipelines, decision deadlock, and unauthorized disruption of legitimate enterprise operations. This paper presents an exhaustive, mathematically formal technical investigation and empirical benchmark of Autonomous SOC architectures. We formalize incident response as a decentralized Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (Dec-POMDP) under dynamic threat uncertainty, model consensus verification over cryptographic remediation DAGs, and establish a dual-tier human-on-the-loop (HOTL) safety gating mechanism. Furthermore, we construct an enterprise SOC evaluation testbed spanning 10,000 multi-stage attack scenarios across real-world enterprise topologies. Our empirical findings demonstrate that our multi-agent autonomous framework slashes Mean Time to Detect (MTTD) from 18.4 minutes to 4.2 seconds and Mean Time to Remediate (MTTR) from 42.6 minutes to 18.2 seconds (a 99.3% reduction) while preserving a 99.6% remediation accuracy against MITRE ATT&CK kill chains. Finally, we formulate open challenges in adversarial prompt-injection resilience, continuous defensive co-evolution, and liability attribution under international cyber law.
